lead: This unit shows how an Android app talks to the outside world: it sends SMS and e-mail, shows maps, reads location, protects user data, ships a signed APK and takes part in m-commerce. After it you can add a map with markers, request location updates, list the main mobile security risks, prepare a release build, and explain a UPI or card payment flow with its fees.
about: Unit 5 moves an app beyond its own screen. Chapter 5.1 sends SMS and e-mail through Android intents and SmsManager. Chapter 5.2 draws Google maps with markers. Chapter 5.3 obtains location fixes and turns them into location-based services. Chapter 5.4 surveys mobile security threats and controls. Chapter 5.5 signs, versions and deploys APK files. Chapter 5.6 explains m-commerce structures, payment flows and fees. The chapters build in that order: messaging and maps create user-facing services, location adds context, security checks the risks, publishing releases the app, and m-commerce shows how the released app earns money. The marked advanced chapters are shorter.

chapters.idea: An app can hand a message to another app or to the phone's SMS service instead of building its own network stack.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter. Cover SMS sending with SmsManager: split long text, call sendTextMessage, handle sent and delivered intents, and request SEND_SMS permission. Cover e-mail with ACTION_SENDTO and ACTION_SEND intents, extras for subject, body and attachment, and the chooser. Some syllabi call this SMS messaging and sending e-mail. Keep code to one screen.

figure.title: SMS send path
figure.aria: A 320-character message is split into 153-character parts, producing three SMS parts that the carrier delivers and the recipient rejoins.

chapters.example: Question: An Android app sends a 320-character SMS in 7-bit GSM encoding. A single SMS carries 160 characters. Each part of a concatenated SMS carries 153 characters because 7 bytes go to the user data header. How many SMS parts are sent? At ₹0.20 per part, what is the cost? Answer: 320 ÷ 153 = 2.09, so 3 parts. Cost = 3 × ₹0.20 = ₹0.60.
chapters.trap: Using 160 characters per part for a long SMS; the concatenation header reduces each part to 153 characters.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 intents and built-in apps; Unit 1 SMS as a mobile service.
chapters.leave: Telecom SMS architecture and GSM/GPRS signalling to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: A map screen asks a map SDK for tiles and draws app data as markers on top.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter. Cover the Google Maps SDK for Android, API key in the manifest, MapFragment versus MapView, CameraUpdate, markers with titles, info windows, map types and lifecycle. Some syllabi call this displaying maps. Do not teach location providers here.

figure.title: Map display path
figure.aria: The app loads a MapFragment, the Maps SDK checks an API key and fetches tiles, then the app adds three markers and moves the camera to show them.

chapters.example: Question: A map screen must show three markers at latitude and longitude (12.0, 77.0), (12.1, 77.2) and (11.9, 77.1). Find the camera center and the latitude and longitude spans so all three fit. Answer: latitude center = (12.1 + 11.9) ÷ 2 = 12.0; longitude center = (77.2 + 77.0) ÷ 2 = 77.1. Latitude span = 12.1 − 11.9 = 0.2; longitude span = 77.2 − 77.0 = 0.2. Move the camera to (12.0, 77.1) and choose a zoom that covers the 0.2° span.
chapters.trap: Swapping latitude and longitude in LatLng; the constructor order is latitude first, longitude second.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 fragments and intents; Unit 3 views.
chapters.leave: GPS provider details to Chapter 3; release key signing to Chapter 5.

chapters.idea: Location-based services turn a stream of position fixes into nearby search, geofencing, tracking or local offers.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter. Cover fine versus coarse permission, GPS/network/passive providers, LocationManager and FusedLocationProviderClient, getLastKnownLocation, requestLocationUpdates with minTime and minDistance, removing updates, accuracy, geocoding and proximity alerts. Some syllabi call this getting location data, monitoring a location and LBS. Do not derive GPS mathematics.

figure.title: Location update pipeline
figure.aria: An app gets runtime location permission, chooses a provider, requests updates every 20 seconds with a 100-metre distance filter, and receives fixes for map or location-based services use.

chapters.example: Question: A delivery app requests location updates every 20 s with a minimum distance of 100 m. A rider moves at 18 km/h. What is the maximum number of updates per minute? How far does the rider move between two time ticks? Answer: 18 km/h = 18000 m ÷ 3600 s = 5 m/s. In 20 s the rider moves 5 × 20 = 100 m, so the distance filter is met at each tick. Maximum updates = 60 ÷ 20 = 3 per minute.
chapters.trap: Manifest permission alone is not enough on modern Android; ask for fine or coarse location at runtime.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 location tracking basics; Unit 2 activity permissions.
chapters.leave: Map drawing to Chapter 2; cellular handover to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Mobile security is the set of threats and controls that protect app code, user data, network traffic and the device itself.
chapters.depth: Cover the mobile threat model: malware, data leakage, unsafe storage, weak permissions, network attacks and device loss. Cover controls: least privilege, runtime permissions, app sandbox, encryption, TLS, screen lock, remote wipe and secure keystore. Mention OWASP Mobile Top 10 as a list name only. Use Android examples.

figure.aria: The tree groups mobile security into app, network and device layers, with controls such as permissions, encrypted storage, TLS, screen lock and remote wipe.

chapters.example: Question: A wallet app uses a 4-digit PIN. How many PINs are possible? At 10 guesses per second with no lockout, how long to try all? If the app locks for 30 s after every 5 wrong guesses, what is the approximate time to try all 10,000 PINs? Answer: 10⁴ = 10,000 PINs. No lockout: 10,000 ÷ 10 = 1,000 s = 16 min 40 s. With lockout: 2,000 groups of 5; 2,000 × 30 s = 60,000 s lock time plus 1,000 s guessing ≈ 61,000 s ≈ 16.9 h.
chapters.trap: Assuming HTTPS protects data at rest; local files and preferences still need encryption or a keystore.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 storage and content providers; Unit 1 wireless risks.
chapters.leave: Payment fraud detail to Chapter 6; signing keys to Chapter 5.

chapters.idea: Publishing means turning a debug app into a signed, versioned release APK and deploying it by a store or direct install.
chapters.depth: Cover release preparation: versionCode and versionName, release keystore, signing, build variants, shrink and minify, release testing, APK versus AAB (Play uses AAB, sideload uses APK), deploying APK via store or direct install, and update rules. Some syllabi call this preparing and publishing an app and deploying APK files. Do not teach UI testing.

figure.title: Release APK pipeline
figure.aria: The release pipeline sets a higher version code, signs the app with the release keystore, builds and tests the APK, then deploys it to a store or by direct install.

chapters.example: Question: An app has versionCode 7 and versionName 1.2.3. You publish one patch update. What are the new versionCode and versionName? Why can versionCode 7 not be uploaded again? Answer: versionCode must increase, so use 8; versionName becomes 1.2.4. Play compares versionCode, and an APK with 7 is not an update over the existing 7.
chapters.trap: Reusing or lowering versionCode; Play rejects it, and losing the upload keystore blocks updates signed with the same identity.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 app creation and SDK; Unit 4 data storage.
chapters.leave: Map API key restrictions to Chapter 2; security review to Chapter 4.

chapters.idea: M-commerce is buying and selling through mobile devices, with a payment chain of customer, merchant, gateway and bank, and fees that decide net revenue.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter. Cover m-commerce structure (consumer, merchant, payment gateway, bank or PSP), pros and cons, mobile payment systems: cards, wallets, UPI and carrier billing. Cover settlement, fees and security. Some syllabi call this mobile payment systems. Keep regulation high-level.

figure.aria: A customer pays ₹1,200 in a merchant app, the payment gateway asks the bank to authorise the payment, and the approval returns to the merchant and customer.

chapters.example: Question: A merchant sells an item for ₹1,200. A card gateway charges 2% plus ₹3 per transaction. A UPI transfer charges 0%. What does the merchant receive after each payment? For 500 card orders, what is the total gateway fee? Answer: card fee = 0.02 × 1,200 + 3 = 24 + 3 = ₹27; merchant receives 1,200 − 27 = ₹1,173. UPI fee = ₹0; merchant receives ₹1,200. For 500 card orders, total fee = 500 × 27 = ₹13,500.
chapters.trap: Comparing gross order value with net revenue; the gateway fee reduces the merchant's receipt.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 mobile networks; Chapter 4 security; Chapter 1 receipts.
chapters.leave: Bank regulation, taxation and detailed UPI protocol to commerce or finance courses.
